category: Numerical integration, differentiation, root finding & differential equations
description: Adaptive quadrature and discrete integration, numerical gradients and Laplacians, scalar root finding and unconstrained minimization, and the full family of ordinary differential equation, differential algebraic, boundary value, delay and 1-D parabolic-elliptic PDE solvers in core MATLAB.

tools.name: integral
tools.description: Numerically integrates a function of one variable using globally adaptive quadrature, handling infinite limits and integrable endpoint singularities. The integrand must accept a vector of x values and return a vector of the same size unless you set ArrayValued. Use it as the default choice for definite integrals of smooth functions.
tools.usage:
q = integral(fun, xmin, xmax)
q = integral(fun, xmin, xmax, Name, Value)

parameters.name: fun
parameters.description: Function handle; must be vectorized unless 'ArrayValued' is true.

parameters.name: xmin, xmax
parameters.description: Limits of integration; may be -Inf and Inf, or complex for contour integration.

parameters.name: 'ArrayValued'
parameters.description: true when fun returns an array for scalar input.

parameters.name: 'Waypoints'
parameters.description: Points the integration path must pass through, useful for discontinuities.

tools.example:
integral(@(x) exp(-x.^2), -Inf, Inf)
sqrt(pi)
integral(@(x) 1./sqrt(x), 0, 1)
integral(@(x) abs(x-0.3), 0, 1, 'Waypoints', 0.3)
integral(@(x) [sin(x); cos(x)], 0, pi, 'ArrayValued', true)
tools.notes: A non-vectorized integrand produces wrong results silently; test with `fun([1 2 3])` first or set 'ArrayValued'. Place known discontinuities in 'Waypoints' rather than relying on the adaptive algorithm to find them.

tools.name: integral2
tools.description: Numerically integrates a function of two variables over a planar region, where the y limits may be function handles of x so the region can be non-rectangular. Two algorithms are available: 'tiled' handles endpoint singularities well and 'iterated' handles infinite domains. Use it for areas, moments, and double integrals in probability.
tools.usage:
q = integral2(fun, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
q = integral2(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: fun
parameters.description: Vectorized function handle fun(x,y) that accepts arrays.

parameters.name: ymin, ymax
parameters.description: Scalars or function handles of x describing the region.

tools.example:
integral2(@(x,y) x.*y, 0, 1, 0, 1)
q = integral2(@(x,y) ones(size(x)), 0, 1, 0, @(x) sqrt(1-x.^2));
[q pi/4]
integral2(@(x,y) exp(-x.^2-y.^2), -Inf, Inf, -Inf, Inf, 'Method', 'iterated')
tools.notes: The integrand must be vectorized in both arguments with elementwise operators. For an infinite domain use 'iterated'; the default 'tiled' method may fail to converge.

tools.name: integral3
tools.description: Numerically integrates a function of three variables over a volume, where the y limits may depend on x and the z limits on both x and y. Use it for volumes, masses, moments of inertia and triple integrals in physics. As with integral2, the integrand must be fully vectorized.
tools.usage:
q = integral3(fun, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax)
q = integral3(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: zmin, zmax
parameters.description: Scalars or functions of x and y.

tools.notes: Triple adaptive quadrature is expensive; for smooth integrands over simple regions, a tensor-product Gauss rule or Monte Carlo sampling can be far faster.

tools.name: trapz
tools.description: Integrates discrete sampled data with the trapezoidal rule, either with unit spacing, a uniform spacing scalar, or explicit sample points. Use it when you have data rather than a function, for example to compute energy from a sampled power signal or area under a measured curve. Accuracy is second order in the spacing.
tools.usage:
Q = trapz(Y)
Q = trapz(X, Y)
Q = trapz(___, dim)

parameters.name: X
parameters.description: Sample points, or a scalar uniform spacing.

tools.notes: For smooth data the trapezoidal rule underestimates convex curves; `cumtrapz` gives the running integral and `integral` is more accurate when a function handle is available.

tools.name: cumtrapz
tools.description: Computes the cumulative trapezoidal integral of sampled data, returning a result the same size as the input with the first element equal to zero. Use it to integrate acceleration into velocity, power into energy, or a density into a cumulative distribution. It respects non-uniform sample spacing when X is supplied.
tools.usage:
Q = cumtrapz(Y)
Q = cumtrapz(X, Y)
Q = cumtrapz(___, dim)
tools.notes: Integrating noisy data twice accumulates drift quickly; high-pass filter or detrend between integrations. The result starts at 0, so add the initial condition yourself.

tools.name: quadgk
tools.description: Integrates with adaptive Gauss-Kronrod quadrature, which is particularly effective for oscillatory integrands, infinite intervals and moderate endpoint singularities. It returns both the value and an error estimate. `integral` calls it internally, but quadgk gives direct access to the error estimate and to contour integration through waypoints.
tools.usage:
q = quadgk(fun, a, b)
[q, errbnd] = quadgk(fun, a, b)
[q, errbnd] = quadgk(fun, a, b, Name, Value)

parameters.name: a, b
parameters.description: Limits; may be infinite or complex.

parameters.name: 'Waypoints'
parameters.description: Intermediate points defining the integration path.

tools.example:
[q, err] = quadgk(@(x) sin(100*x)./x, 1, 10);
[q err]
quadgk(@(z) 1./z, 1, 1, 'Waypoints', [1i, -1, -1i])
quadgk(@(x) exp(-x.^2), 0, Inf)
tools.notes: Use the 'Waypoints' option with complex points to perform contour integration in the complex plane. For most everyday integrals, `integral` is the friendlier interface.

tools.name: quad2d
tools.description: Integrates a function of two variables over a planar region using a tiled adaptive algorithm, returning both the result and an error estimate. It handles regions whose y limits are functions of x and copes well with singularities along the boundary. Use it when you want the explicit error bound that `integral2` does not return.
tools.usage:
q = quad2d(fun, a, b, c, d)
[q, errbnd] = quad2d(___)
[q, errbnd] = quad2d(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: c, d
parameters.description: Limits in y; may be function handles of x.

parameters.name: 'Singular'
parameters.description: true (default) to use transformations that handle boundary singularities.

tools.notes: quad2d requires finite limits; use `integral2` with the 'iterated' method for infinite domains.

tools.name: gradient
tools.description: Computes numerical gradients of sampled data using central differences in the interior and one-sided differences at the edges, returning arrays the same size as the input. For a matrix it returns the x and y partial derivatives. Use it for slope fields, quiver plots of scalar fields and estimating derivatives from measurements.
tools.usage:
FX = gradient(F)
[FX, FY] = gradient(F)
[FX, FY, FZ, ...] = gradient(F)
[___] = gradient(F, h)
[___] = gradient(F, hx, hy, ...)

parameters.name: hx, hy
parameters.description: Spacing or coordinate vectors for each dimension.

tools.notes: For a matrix, the first output is the derivative along columns (the x direction in meshgrid orientation), which is the opposite of what many people expect. gradient keeps the input size, unlike `diff`.

tools.name: del2
tools.description: Computes a discrete Laplacian, the sum of the second derivatives divided by 2*N for an N-dimensional array, with one-sided formulas at the boundary. Use it for heat and diffusion simulations, for edge detection, and for checking whether a field satisfies Laplace's equation. Multiply by 4 in 2-D to obtain the conventional Laplacian.
tools.usage:
L = del2(U)
L = del2(U, h)
L = del2(U, hx, hy, ...)

parameters.name: hx, hy
parameters.description: Spacing or coordinate vectors per dimension.

tools.notes: The scaling factor of 1/(2*N) is a long-standing MATLAB convention that surprises people; multiply by 2*N to recover the mathematical Laplacian. For sparse matrix operators use `delsq` with `numgrid`.

tools.name: fzero
tools.description: Finds a root of a continuous function of one variable, starting either from an initial guess or from a bracketing interval where the function changes sign. Given a sign-changing bracket it is guaranteed to converge, combining bisection, secant and inverse quadratic interpolation. Use it for solving scalar nonlinear equations without an optimization toolbox.
tools.usage:
x = fzero(fun, x0)
x = fzero(fun, [a b])
x = fzero(fun, x0, options)
[x, fval, exitflag, output] = fzero(___)

parameters.name: x0
parameters.description: Initial guess, or a two-element bracket with opposite function signs.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Structure from `optimset` with fields such as TolX and Display.

tools.example:
fzero(@cos, 1)
fzero(@(x) x.^3 - 2*x - 5, [2 3])
[x, fval, flag] = fzero(@(x) exp(x) - 3, 1);
[x fval flag]
fzero(@(x) x.^2, [-1 1])   % no sign change: error
tools.notes: fzero cannot find roots of even multiplicity such as x^2, because the function does not change sign. Use `roots` for polynomials and `fsolve` (Optimization Toolbox) for systems.

tools.name: fminsearch
tools.description: Minimizes an unconstrained multivariable function using the derivative-free Nelder-Mead simplex algorithm. It is robust for noisy, non-smooth or non-differentiable objectives, but converges slowly and only finds a local minimum. Use it for small problems, typically fewer than about ten variables, where gradients are unavailable.
tools.usage:
x = fminsearch(fun, x0)
x = fminsearch(fun, x0, options)
[x, fval, exitflag, output] = fminsearch(___)

parameters.name: fun
parameters.description: Objective function handle taking a vector and returning a scalar.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: `optimset` structure with TolX, TolFun, MaxIter, MaxFunEvals, Display, PlotFcns.

tools.notes: Nelder-Mead has no convergence guarantee and handles no constraints; bound variables by transforming them, for example optimizing log of a positive parameter. Restart from the returned point to tighten a solution.

tools.name: fminbnd
tools.description: Finds a local minimum of a function of one variable within a fixed interval, using golden section search and parabolic interpolation. Use it for line searches, for one-dimensional calibration and for any scalar minimization where you can bracket the answer. It never evaluates outside the given interval, which makes it safe for functions that are undefined elsewhere.
tools.usage:
x = fminbnd(fun, x1, x2)
x = fminbnd(fun, x1, x2, options)
[x, fval, exitflag, output] = fminbnd(___)
tools.example:
[x, fval] = fminbnd(@(x) (x-2).^2 + 1, 0, 5)
fminbnd(@(x) -sin(x), 0, pi)
fminbnd(@(x) x.^2, -1, 1, optimset('TolX', 1e-12))
tools.notes: If the minimum lies at an endpoint, fminbnd returns that endpoint with exitflag 1 but the result is a boundary solution, not an interior stationary point. To maximize, minimize the negated function.

tools.name: optimset
tools.description: Creates or modifies the options structure used by `fzero`, `fminsearch` and `fminbnd`. Call it with no arguments to see the available fields and defaults. Use `optimget` to read a value back out of an options structure.
tools.usage:
options = optimset
options = optimset(Name, Value, ...)
options = optimset(oldopts, Name, Value, ...)
val = optimget(options, Name)

parameters.name: 'TolFun'
parameters.description: Termination tolerance on the function value.

tools.notes: Optimization Toolbox solvers use the newer `optimoptions` interface instead; `optimset` remains the correct choice for the core MATLAB solvers listed here.

tools.name: ode45
tools.description: Solves non-stiff ordinary differential equations with an explicit Runge-Kutta (4,5) Dormand-Prince pair and adaptive step size. It is the recommended first solver to try for a new problem. The solution structure form works with `deval` for dense output at arbitrary times.
tools.usage:
[t, y] = ode45(odefun, tspan, y0)
[t, y] = ode45(odefun, tspan, y0, options)
[t, y, te, ye, ie] = ode45(___)
sol = ode45(___)

parameters.name: odefun
parameters.description: Function handle dydt = f(t,y) returning a column vector.

parameters.name: tspan
parameters.description: [t0 tf] for automatic steps, or a vector of output times.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Structure from `odeset`: RelTol, AbsTol, Events, MaxStep, OutputFcn, Mass, NonNegative.

tools.notes: If ode45 takes tiny steps or runs for a very long time, the problem is probably stiff: switch to `ode15s`. Passing a vector of times in tspan does not change the internal steps, only where output is reported.

tools.name: ode23
tools.description: Solves non-stiff ODEs with an explicit Bogacki-Shampine Runge-Kutta (2,3) pair. It is lower order than ode45 and therefore takes more steps for tight tolerances, but each step is cheaper, which makes it competitive at crude tolerances or on mildly stiff problems. The interface is identical to ode45.
tools.usage:
[t, y] = ode23(odefun, tspan, y0)
[t, y] = ode23(odefun, tspan, y0, options)
sol = ode23(___)
tools.notes: Prefer ode23 when the tolerance is loose or the right-hand side is expensive but the solution is not smooth; otherwise ode45 is usually more efficient.

tools.name: ode113
tools.description: Solves non-stiff ODEs with a variable-order Adams-Bashforth-Moulton predictor-corrector method. Because it reuses previous solution values, it needs far fewer function evaluations per step than Runge-Kutta methods, which pays off when the right-hand side is expensive and the solution is smooth. It is the classic choice for orbital mechanics and long smooth integrations at tight tolerances.
tools.usage:
[t, y] = ode113(odefun, tspan, y0)
[t, y] = ode113(odefun, tspan, y0, options)
sol = ode113(___)
tools.notes: Multistep methods restart after every discontinuity or event, which is expensive; prefer a Runge-Kutta solver for problems with frequent events.

tools.name: ode15s
tools.description: Solves stiff ODEs and differential algebraic equations of index 1 using variable-order numerical differentiation formulas. It is the workhorse for chemical kinetics, circuit simulation and any system with widely separated time constants. Supplying an analytic Jacobian through `odeset` typically makes it several times faster.
tools.usage:
[t, y] = ode15s(odefun, tspan, y0)
[t, y] = ode15s(odefun, tspan, y0, options)
sol = ode15s(___)

parameters.name: options.Jacobian
parameters.description: Analytic Jacobian matrix or function handle.

parameters.name: options.JPattern
parameters.description: Sparsity pattern of the Jacobian for large systems.

parameters.name: options.Mass
parameters.description: Mass matrix M for M*y' = f(t,y), enabling DAE solution.

parameters.name: options.MaxOrder
parameters.description: Maximum order of the NDF formulas, 1 to 5.

tools.notes: For a DAE, the mass matrix must be singular and the initial conditions consistent; use `decic` to compute consistent conditions. `ode23s` may be faster when the problem is stiff but crude accuracy suffices.

tools.name: ode23s
tools.description: Solves stiff ODEs with a modified Rosenbrock formula of order 2, evaluating the Jacobian at every step. It is a one-step method, so it handles frequent discontinuities better than ode15s, and it can be faster at crude tolerances. A constant mass matrix is supported but not a time-dependent one.
tools.usage:
[t, y] = ode23s(odefun, tspan, y0)
[t, y] = ode23s(odefun, tspan, y0, options)
sol = ode23s(___)

parameters.name: options.Jacobian
parameters.description: Analytic Jacobian; strongly recommended for this solver.

tools.notes: Because it forms the Jacobian at every step, ode23s is expensive for large systems unless the Jacobian is cheap or sparse. ode23t and ode23tb are alternatives for moderately stiff problems.

tools.name: ode23t
tools.description: Solves moderately stiff ODEs and DAEs with the trapezoidal rule using a free interpolant. The method has no numerical damping, so it preserves oscillatory energy, which makes it the right choice for structural dynamics and other conservative systems that must not be artificially damped. It also solves DAEs with a singular mass matrix.
tools.usage:
[t, y] = ode23t(odefun, tspan, y0)
[t, y] = ode23t(odefun, tspan, y0, options)
sol = ode23t(___)

parameters.name: options.Mass
parameters.description: Mass matrix, possibly singular for DAEs.

tools.notes: Zero numerical damping is a double-edged property: it preserves oscillations but does not suppress spurious high-frequency modes. Use ode23tb or ode15s when damping is desirable.

tools.name: ode23tb
tools.description: Solves stiff ODEs with an implicit Runge-Kutta formula combining a trapezoidal first stage and a backward differentiation second stage (TR-BDF2). It often outperforms ode15s at crude tolerances and is robust on problems with strong transients. It supports mass matrices and Jacobian options like the other stiff solvers.
tools.usage:
[t, y] = ode23tb(odefun, tspan, y0)
[t, y] = ode23tb(odefun, tspan, y0, options)
sol = ode23tb(___)
tools.notes: Try ode15s, ode23tb and ode23s on a representative case and compare timings; which stiff solver wins is very problem dependent.

tools.name: ode15i
tools.description: Solves fully implicit differential equations of the form f(t, y, y') = 0, where the derivative cannot be isolated. Use it for implicit DAEs arising in multibody dynamics and circuit equations that no mass-matrix formulation can express. Consistent initial values for both y and y' are required, which `decic` can compute.
tools.usage:
[t, y] = ode15i(odefun, tspan, y0, yp0)
[t, y] = ode15i(odefun, tspan, y0, yp0, options)
sol = ode15i(___)

parameters.name: odefun
parameters.description: Residual function handle f(t,y,yp) that must be driven to zero.

parameters.name: y0, yp0
parameters.description: Consistent initial values of the state and its derivative.

parameters.name: options.Jacobian
parameters.description: Cell array {dfdy, dfdyp} of analytic Jacobians.

tools.notes: Initial values that do not satisfy the residual cause an immediate failure; always run `decic` unless you are certain they are consistent.

tools.name: ode78
tools.description: Solves non-stiff ODEs with a high-order explicit Runge-Kutta (7,8) Verner pair, introduced in R2021b. It is more efficient than ode45 at tight tolerances and on smooth problems, because the higher order lets it take much larger steps. Use it for long, accurate integrations of smooth non-stiff systems.
tools.usage:
[t, y] = ode78(odefun, tspan, y0)
[t, y] = ode78(odefun, tspan, y0, options)
sol = ode78(___)
tools.notes: High-order methods lose their advantage when the solution is not smooth or when tolerances are loose; compare against ode45 on your own problem. `ode89` is the even higher order option.

tools.name: ode89
tools.description: Solves non-stiff ODEs with an explicit Runge-Kutta (8,9) Verner pair, the highest-order explicit solver in MATLAB. It is designed for very tight tolerances on smooth problems, such as high-precision orbital propagation. At loose tolerances it is slower than ode45 because of the many stages per step.
tools.usage:
[t, y] = ode89(odefun, tspan, y0)
[t, y] = ode89(odefun, tspan, y0, options)
sol = ode89(___)

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: `odeset` structure; RelTol below 1e-10 is where ode89 shines.

tools.notes: Available since R2021b. Requesting tolerances near machine epsilon is futile because round-off dominates; RelTol around 1e-13 is a practical floor.

tools.name: odeset
tools.description: Creates or modifies the options structure passed to every ODE, DAE and DDE solver. Call it with no output to print all option names and their defaults. Use it to set tolerances, event functions, Jacobians, mass matrices, output functions and step-size limits.
tools.usage:
options = odeset
options = odeset(Name, Value, ...)
options = odeset(oldopts, Name, Value, ...)

parameters.name: 'AbsTol'
parameters.description: Absolute tolerance, scalar or per-component vector; default 1e-6.

parameters.name: 'Events'
parameters.description: Function handle [value, isterminal, direction] = e(t,y) for event location.

parameters.name: 'Jacobian', 'JPattern'
parameters.description: Analytic Jacobian or its sparsity pattern for stiff solvers.

parameters.name: 'Mass', 'MStateDependence'
parameters.description: Mass matrix and how it depends on the state.

parameters.name: 'NonNegative'
parameters.description: Indices of components constrained to be nonnegative.

parameters.name: 'OutputFcn', 'Refine'
parameters.description: Per-step callback and output densification factor.

tools.notes: AbsTol can be a vector so that components with very different magnitudes are each resolved properly. `odeget` reads a single option value back out of the structure.

tools.name: odeget
tools.description: Reads the value of a named option from an ODE options structure, returning a supplied default when the option has not been set. Use it inside custom output functions, event functions or solver wrappers that need to respect the caller's settings. It performs the same case-insensitive partial name matching as `odeset`.
tools.usage:
val = odeget(options, name)
val = odeget(options, name, default)

parameters.name: default
parameters.description: Value returned when the option is empty or unset.

tools.example:
opts = odeset('RelTol', 1e-8);
odeget(opts, 'RelTol')
odeget(opts, 'AbsTol')
odeget(opts, 'AbsTol', 1e-6)
tools.notes: An unset option returns [], which is why the third argument matters when you need a concrete default in wrapper code.

tools.name: deval
tools.description: Evaluates the continuous extension of a solution structure returned by an ODE, BVP or DDE solver at arbitrary points, using the solver's own interpolant. This gives full solver accuracy between the steps that were actually taken, unlike interpolating the output arrays. It can also return derivatives and select individual components.
tools.usage:
sxint = deval(sol, xint)
sxint = deval(sol, xint, idx)
[sxint, spxint] = deval(___)
sxint = deval(xint, sol)

parameters.name: sol
parameters.description: Solution structure from ode45, bvp4c, dde23 and similar.

parameters.name: idx
parameters.description: Indices of the components to return.

tools.notes: Evaluating outside the solution interval extrapolates and triggers a warning. Requesting `sol` output from the solver costs nothing extra and is usually better than passing a dense tspan.

tools.name: ode
tools.description: Creates an ODE problem object (since R2023b) that bundles the equations, initial conditions, parameters, solver choice and options in one place. MATLAB can select a suitable solver automatically, and the object is solved with `solve` or converted to a callable interpolant with `solutionFcn`. Use it when you want a reusable problem definition, easy parameter sweeps, or automatic solver selection.
tools.usage:
F = ode
F = ode(PropertyName=Value, ...)
S = solve(F, tspan)
S = solve(F, t0, tf)
fcn = solutionFcn(F, t0, tf)

parameters.name: ODEFcn
parameters.description: Function handle f(t,y) or f(t,y,p) for the right-hand side.

parameters.name: Parameters
parameters.description: Extra parameters passed to ODEFcn as a third argument.

parameters.name: Solver
parameters.description: Explicit solver name such as "ode45" or "ode15s"; the default is "auto".

parameters.name: EventDefinition, MassMatrix, Jacobian
parameters.description: Event, mass matrix and Jacobian specifications.

tools.notes: Requires R2023b or later. `selectSolver` reports or changes the chosen solver and `consistentInitialConditions` replaces `decic` for DAE initialization.

tools.name: bvp4c
tools.description: Solves two-point boundary value problems for ODEs with a collocation method that is fourth-order accurate and produces a C1-continuous solution. You supply the ODE, a residual function for the boundary conditions, and an initial guess mesh from `bvpinit`. Use it for beam deflection, steady-state transport and shooting-free solution of BVPs.
tools.usage:
sol = bvp4c(odefun, bcfun, solinit)
sol = bvp4c(odefun, bcfun, solinit, options)

parameters.name: odefun
parameters.description: dydx = f(x,y) or f(x,y,p) with unknown parameters.

parameters.name: bcfun
parameters.description: res = bc(ya, yb) returning the boundary condition residuals.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: `bvpset` structure with RelTol, AbsTol, FJacobian, BCJacobian, NMax, Stats.

tools.notes: BVPs can have several solutions; the one you get depends on the initial guess, so try different guesses. `bvp5c` uses a different error control and can be better for very tight tolerances.

tools.name: bvp5c
tools.description: Solves two-point boundary value problems with a four-stage Lobatto IIIa collocation formula, controlling the true error rather than the residual. It is generally more accurate than bvp4c at tight tolerances but does not support unknown parameters in singular problems as flexibly. The calling interface matches bvp4c.
tools.usage:
sol = bvp5c(odefun, bcfun, solinit)
sol = bvp5c(odefun, bcfun, solinit, options)
tools.notes: bvp5c controls the error in the solution itself, so its RelTol means something slightly different from bvp4c's residual control. Neither solver handles problems with a singular coefficient at an endpoint without the SingularTerm option.

tools.name: bvpinit
tools.description: Builds the initial guess structure required by `bvp4c` and `bvp5c`, from a mesh plus either a constant vector, a function of x, or a previously computed solution. Continuation from a solved nearby problem is the standard way to solve hard BVPs. It also carries initial guesses for unknown parameters.
tools.usage:
solinit = bvpinit(x, yinit)
solinit = bvpinit(x, yinit, params)
solinit = bvpinit(sol, [anew bnew])
solinit = bvpinit(sol, [anew bnew], params)

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Initial mesh, a vector of increasing points.

parameters.name: yinit
parameters.description: Constant guess vector or a function handle yinit(x).

parameters.name: sol
parameters.description: Previous solution structure used to extend or continue.

tools.notes: A coarse mesh is fine because the solvers refine adaptively; the quality of the guess matters far more than its resolution. For parameter continuation, feed the previous `sol` back into bvpinit.

tools.name: pdepe
tools.description: Solves initial-boundary value problems for systems of parabolic and elliptic partial differential equations in one space variable and time. You supply three functions describing the PDE coefficients, the initial condition and the boundary conditions in MATLAB's standard flux form. Use it for heat conduction, diffusion and reaction-diffusion problems on a line or in symmetric cylindrical or spherical geometry.
tools.usage:
sol = pdepe(m, pdefun, icfun, bcfun, xmesh, tspan)
sol = pdepe(___, options)

parameters.name: pdefun
parameters.description: [c, f, s] = pdefun(x,t,u,dudx) giving the capacity, flux and source terms.

tools.notes: pdepe handles only one spatial dimension and requires at least one parabolic equation in the system; purely hyperbolic problems are not supported. For 2-D and 3-D PDEs use Partial Differential Equation Toolbox.

tools.name: dde23
tools.description: Solves delay differential equations with one or more constant delays, tracking the discontinuities that propagate from the history function. You supply the right-hand side as f(t, y, Z) where Z holds the delayed states. Use it for control loops with transport lag, population models with maturation delay and networks with signal propagation time.
tools.usage:
sol = dde23(ddefun, lags, history, tspan)
sol = dde23(ddefun, lags, history, tspan, options)

parameters.name: ddefun
parameters.description: dydt = f(t, y, Z) where Z(:,j) is y(t - lags(j)).

parameters.name: history
parameters.description: Solution for t <= t0: a constant vector, a function handle, or a previous solution structure.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: `ddeset` structure with RelTol, AbsTol, Events, Jumps.

tools.notes: Discontinuities in the derivative at t0 propagate to t0+lag, t0+2*lag and so on; dde23 tracks them automatically, which is why a plain ODE solver cannot be used. `ddesd` handles state-dependent and time-varying delays.

tools.name: ddesd
tools.description: Solves delay differential equations with general, possibly state-dependent delays specified by a function that returns the delayed times directly. Use it when the delay depends on the solution or varies with time, as in variable transport speed or threshold-triggered models. The interface mirrors `dde23` but replaces the constant lag vector with a delay function.
tools.usage:
sol = ddesd(ddefun, delays, history, tspan)
sol = ddesd(ddefun, delays, history, tspan, options)

parameters.name: ddefun
parameters.description: dydt = f(t, y, Z) with Z holding the delayed states.

parameters.name: delays
parameters.description: Function handle d = delays(t, y) returning the delayed times, or a constant vector.

tools.notes: The delay function returns times, not lags, which is the opposite convention from `dde23`. ddesd does not track propagated discontinuities as precisely as dde23, so use dde23 when the delays really are constant.
